The Zaporozhets–Tarasov Conjecture on Mean Distances

Journal: arXiv
Eric Shen Email: erick.2013@yandex.ru Address: Moscow State University, Moscow, 119991, Russia
Institute for Numerical Mathematics, Russian Academy of Sciences, Russia
August 2026
Abstract

For a convex body K⊂ℝdK\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} let Δ⁡(K)\Delta(K) be the expected distance between two independent uniform points of KK, and let θ⁡(K)\theta(K) be the expected distance between two uniform points on ∂K\partial K. The Zaporozhets–Tarasov conjecture asserts Δ⁡(K)≤θ⁡(K)\Delta(K)\leq\theta(K). We prove this conjecture in case d=2d=2. In addition, we give a six-vertex convex polytope in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3} for which the reverse strict inequality holds, and obtain counterexamples in every dimension d≥3d\geq 3 by taking products with segments. This settles the conjecture in every dimension d≥2d\geq 2. Finally, we show that θ⁡(K)>per⁡K6\theta(K)>\frac{\operatorname{per}K}{6} for every planar convex body.

MSC2020: 52A40, 60D05, 52A22

Keywords: 
convex body; mean distance; Gini mean difference; Zaporozhets–Tarasov conjecture.

1 Introduction

Let K⊂ℝdK\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a compact convex body. The conjecture of Zaporozhets and Tarasov asks whether

Δ⁡(K):=𝔼​|X1−X2|≤𝔼|B1−B2|=:θ⁡(K)\Delta(K):=\mathbb{E}|X_{1}-X_{2}|\leq\mathbb{E}|B_{1}-B_{2}|=:\theta(K)

for every convex body K⊂ℝdK\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}, where X1,X2X_{1},X_{2} are uniform in KK with respect to the normalized Lebesgue measure and B1,B2B_{1},B_{2} are uniform on ∂K\partial K with respect to the normalized arclength measure.

Lotnikov proved the planar centrally symmetric case and an analogue for sufficiently high moments in arbitrary dimension [2]. Tokmachev proved the conjecture, in fact a convex-order statement, for planar bodies whose area and boundary centroids coincide and for a class of circumscribed polytopes [4]. Related extremal questions for Δ\Delta and θ\theta were studied in [1, 3]. In particular, Bonnet, Gusakova, Thäle and Zaporozhets proved the sharp inequalities

760<Δ⁡(K)per⁡K<16\frac{7}{60}<\frac{\Delta(K)}{\operatorname{per}K}<\frac{1}{6}

for planar convex bodies [1], where per⁡K\operatorname{per}K stands for perimeter of KK. It is also shown that the upper bound is approached by thin rectangles converging to a doubled segment. According to Tokmachev [4, Eq. (5)], Gusakova and Zaporozhets suggested an analogous pair of inequalities for θ\theta

16<θ⁡(K)per⁡K≤2π2.\frac{1}{6}<\frac{\theta(K)}{\operatorname{per}K}\leq\frac{2}{\pi^{2}}.

The upper bound, with equality only for the disk, was proved by Tokmachev [3]; we prove the lower bound, see Theorem 5.17.

Prior to that, we prove the Zaporozhets-Tarasov conjecture in the case d=2d=2, see Corollary 3.10. The result is mostly self-contained, in particular, it does not use the aforementioned inequalities on Δ⁡(K)\Delta(K) from [1] and is obtained as a corollary of a more general statement, see Theorem 2.3. We also prove an analogous inequality for the second moment, see Corollary 3.11. In addition to that, we show that the conjecture is false in every dimension d≥3d\geq 3, see Example 4.13, Figure 1 and Proposition 4.16.

Definition 1.1.

For a probability measure ρ\rho on ℝ\mathbb{R}, write

𝒟⁡(ρ)=∬ℝ2|x−y|​𝑑ρ​(x)​𝑑ρ​(y).\mathcal{D}(\rho)=\iint_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}|x-y|\,d\rho(x)d\rho(y).

This is the Gini mean difference of ρ\rho.

We slightly abuse this notation throughout the text, writing 𝒟⁡(X)\mathcal{D}(X) with XX being a random variable or a probability density. In either case, 𝒟⁡(X)\mathcal{D}(X) is understood as 𝒟⁡(ρX)\mathcal{D}(\rho_{X}), where ρX\rho_{X} denotes the corresponding probability measure. For basic properties of the Gini mean difference used throughout the paper we refer the reader to [6]. The main result immediately follows from a stronger directional inequality.

Theorem 1.2.

Let K⊂ℝ2K\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} be a convex body. Fix a unit vector uu. Let pup_{u} be the pushforward of normalized area measure on KK under x↦⟨x,u⟩x\mapsto\langle x,u\rangle, and let quq_{u} be the corresponding pushforward of normalized arclength measure on ∂K\partial K. Then

𝒟⁡(qu)≥𝒟⁡(pu).\mathcal{D}(q_{u})\geq\mathcal{D}(p_{u}). (1.1)

We first prove the theorem for smooth strictly convex bodies and the general case follows by approximation.

Plan. After rotating and rescaling, the projection of KK is [0,1][0,1] and

K={(x,y):0≤x≤1,g(x)≤y≤f(x)},K=\{(x,y):0\leq x\leq 1,\ g(x)\leq y\leq f(x)\},

where ff is concave and gg is convex. Put

W=f−g,a=f′,b=g′.W=f-g,\qquad a=f^{\prime},\qquad b=g^{\prime}.

The projected area density is proportional to WW, while the projected boundary density is proportional to

1+a2+1+b2.\sqrt{1+a^{2}}+\sqrt{1+b^{2}}.

The proof has two steps. First, we find two densities φ\varphi and ψ\psi, nonincreasing and nondecreasing, respectively, such that the projected arclength density qq satisfies q=φ+ψ2q=\frac{\varphi+\psi}{2} while the projected area density pp is proportional to the difference of the CDFs of φ\varphi and ψ\psi. Then we apply a one-dimensional Theorem saying that an endpoint mixture is more dispersed than the normalized occupation measure between the endpoints. The only substantial step is the second one, to which we now turn.

2 The monotone-endpoint theorem

Theorem 2.3.

Let φ\varphi be a nonincreasing probability density and ψ\psi a nondecreasing probability density on [0,1][0,1]. Let

Φ⁡(x)=∫0xφ⁡(s)​𝑑s,Ψ⁡(x)=∫0xψ⁡(s)​𝑑s.\Phi(x)=\int_{0}^{x}\varphi(s)\,ds,\qquad\Psi(x)=\int_{0}^{x}\psi(s)\,ds.

Put

H=Φ−Ψ,A=∫01H⁡(x)​𝑑x,H=\Phi-\Psi,\qquad A=\int_{0}^{1}H(x)\,dx,

and assume A>0A>0. Define

p⁡(x)=H⁡(x)A,q⁡(x)=φ⁡(x)+ψ⁡(x)2.p(x)=\frac{H(x)}{A},\qquad q(x)=\frac{\varphi(x)+\psi(x)}{2}.

Then

𝒟⁡(q)≥𝒟⁡(p).\mathcal{D}(q)\geq\mathcal{D}(p).

Since Φ\Phi is concave and Ψ\Psi is convex, Φ⁡(x)≥x≥Ψ⁡(x)\Phi(x)\geq x\geq\Psi(x). Thus H≥0H\geq 0, and pp is indeed a probability density.

Remark 2.4.

There is also a geometric reformulation. Let x​(u)=Φ−1​(u)x(u)=\Phi^{-1}(u) and y​(u)=Ψ−1​(u)y(u)=\Psi^{-1}(u). If U∼Unif⁡[0,1]U\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1], then x⁡(U)∼φ,y⁡(U)∼ψx(U)\sim\varphi,\,\,y(U)\sim\psi. Consider

L={(u,z):0≤u≤1,x(u)≤z≤y(u)}.L=\{(u,z):0\leq u\leq 1,\ x(u)\leq z\leq y(u)\}.

Since xx is convex and yy is concave, LL is convex. Choosing one of the two endpoints of the (uniformly distributed) vertical slice [x⁡(U),y⁡(U)][x(U),y(U)] with equal probability gives the law qq. Schematically,

q⁡(z)​𝑑z=12​∫01(δx⁡(u)+δy⁡(u))​(𝑑z)​𝑑u.q(z)dz=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}\bigl(\delta_{x(u)}+\delta_{y(u)}\bigr)(dz)\,du.

On the other hand, the length of the horizontal section of LL at height zz is

|{u:x⁡(u)≤z≤y⁡(u)}|=Φ⁡(z)−Ψ⁡(z)=H⁡(z).\bigl|\{u:x(u)\leq z\leq y(u)\}\bigr|=\Phi(z)-\Psi(z)=H(z).

Consequently, pp is the second-coordinate distribution of a uniform point of LL, that is, choose a slice with a probability proportional to its length and then a random point in it. Explicitly,

p⁡(z)​d​z=∫01𝟏{x(u)≤z≤y(u)}du∫01(y⁡(u)−x⁡(u))​𝑑u​d​z.p(z)\,dz=\frac{\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\mathbf{1}_{\{x(u)\leq z\leq y(u)\}}\,du}{\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}(y(u)-x(u))\,du}\,dz.

Every decreasing probability density on [0,1][0,1] is a mixture of uniform densities on intervals [0,t][0,t], as shown by the following Proposition. This is a one-sided form of Khintchine’s representation theorem for unimodal distributions, see [5].

Proposition 2.5.

Let φ\varphi be a probability density on [0,1][0,1] admitting a nonincreasing representative, which we also denote by φ\varphi. There is a random variable T∈[0,1]T\in[0,1] such that, for U∼Unif⁡[0,1]U\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1] independent of TT, the variable

X=T​UX=TU

has density φ\varphi. Likewise, for every nondecreasing density ψ\psi, there is S∈[0,1]S\in[0,1] such that

Y=1−S​V,V∼Unif⁡[0,1],Y=1-SV,\qquad V\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1],

has density ψ\psi.

Proof.

As the law of TT one may take the Stieltjes mixing measure

ρ⁡(d​t)=−t​d​φ​(t)+φ⁡(1−)​δ1​(d​t),\rho(dt)=-t\,d\varphi(t)+\varphi(1-)\delta_{1}(dt),

for which

φ⁡(x)=∫[x,1]1t​ρ​(𝑑t)for a.e. ​x∈(0,1).\varphi(x)=\int_{[x,1]}\frac{1}{t}\,\rho(dt)\quad\text{for a.e. }x\in(0,1).

As φ\varphi is nonincreasing, ρ\rho is nonnegative and the Stieltjes integration by parts gives ρ⁡([0,1])=∫01φ=1.\rho([0,1])=\int_{0}^{1}\varphi=1. ∎

Next lemma gives a lower bound on the Gini mean difference of qq in terms of its mean and auxiliary variables.

Lemma 2.6.

In the notation of Theorem 2.3 and Proposition 2.5, denote

A=∫01(Φ−Ψ)=𝔼​Y−𝔼​X=1−𝔼​T+𝔼​S2.A=\int_{0}^{1}(\Phi-\Psi)=\mathbb{E}Y-\mathbb{E}X=1-\frac{\mathbb{E}T+\mathbb{E}S}{2}.

Then 𝒟⁡(q)≥13​B:=13​(1−A+32​A2+Var⁡(T)+Var⁡(S)).\mathcal{D}(q)\geq\frac{1}{3}B:=\frac{1}{3}(1-A+\frac{3}{2}A^{2}+\operatorname{Var}(T)+\operatorname{Var}(S)).

Proof.

Take U,U′∼Unif⁡[0,1]U,U^{\prime}\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1] independent. Then for s,t∈[0,1]s,t\in[0,1], direct integration gives

𝔼​|t​U−s​U′|=t+s6+(t−s)23​max⁡(t,s),\mathbb{E}|tU-sU^{\prime}|=\frac{t+s}{6}+\frac{(t-s)^{2}}{3\max(t,s)},

with the second term read as zero when s=t=0s=t=0. Since max⁡(s,t)≤1\max(s,t)\leq 1,

𝔼​|t​U−s​U′|≥t+s6+(t−s)23.\mathbb{E}|tU-sU^{\prime}|\geq\frac{t+s}{6}+\frac{(t-s)^{2}}{3}.

Now invoke Proposition 2.5:

𝒟⁡(X)=𝔼​|T​U−T′​U′|=𝔼T,T′​𝔼​(|T​U−T′​U′||T,T′)≥𝔼⁡(T+T′6+(T−T′)23).\mathcal{D}(X)=\mathbb{E}|TU-T^{\prime}U^{\prime}|=\mathbb{E}_{T,T^{\prime}}\mathbb{E}(|TU-T^{\prime}U^{\prime}|\,|\,T,T^{\prime})\geq\mathbb{E}(\frac{T+T^{\prime}}{6}+\frac{(T-T^{\prime})^{2}}{3}).

Using that TT and T′T^{\prime} are independent and applying the same argument to YY one obtains

𝒟⁡(X)≥𝔼​T3+23​Var​T,𝒟⁡(Y)≥𝔼​S3+23​Var​S.\mathcal{D}(X)\geq\frac{\mathbb{E}T}{3}+\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{Var}T,\qquad\mathcal{D}(Y)\geq\frac{\mathbb{E}S}{3}+\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{Var}S. (2.1)

For independent laws on the line with finite first moments with distribution functions Φ,Ψ\Phi,\Psi,

2​𝔼​|X−Y|−𝒟⁡(X)−𝒟⁡(Y)=2​∫ℝ(Φ−Ψ)2.2\mathbb{E}|X-Y|-\mathcal{D}(X)-\mathcal{D}(Y)=2\int_{\mathbb{R}}(\Phi-\Psi)^{2}.

This follows immediately from the standard CDF formulas for the three terms. Since qq is an equal-probability mixture of XX and YY, we have

𝒟⁡(q)=𝒟⁡(X)+𝒟⁡(Y)2+12​∫01H​(x)2​𝑑x.\mathcal{D}(q)=\frac{\mathcal{D}(X)+\mathcal{D}(Y)}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{1}H(x)^{2}\,dx. (2.2)

By Cauchy–Schwarz, ∫H2≥A2\int H^{2}\geq A^{2}. Finally, using (2.1), and (2.2), we obtain

𝒟⁡(q)≥16​(𝔼​T+𝔼​S+2​Var⁡T+2​Var⁡S)+12​A2=13​B.\mathcal{D}(q)\geq\frac{1}{6}(\mathbb{E}T+\mathbb{E}S+2\operatorname{Var}T+2\operatorname{Var}S)+\frac{1}{2}A^{2}=\frac{1}{3}B. (2.3)

∎

Lemma 2.7.

Let pp be as in Theorem 2.3, let ZZ have density pp, and assume BB as in Lemma 2.6. Then

12​Var⁡Z≤B2.12\operatorname{Var}Z\leq B^{2}.

If PP denotes the CDF of ZZ, then by the Gini covariance identity

𝒟⁡(p)=4​Cov⁡(Z,P⁡(Z)).\mathcal{D}(p)=4\operatorname{Cov}(Z,P(Z)).

Since pp is absolutely continuous, P⁡(Z)P(Z) is uniform on [0,1][0,1]. Consequently, using Cauchy–Schwarz again,

𝒟⁡(p)≤4​Var⁡(Z)​Var⁡(P⁡(Z)CLOSE=4​Var⁡(Z)​112=23​Var⁡Z.\mathcal{D}(p)\leq 4\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(Z)\operatorname{Var}(P(Z)}=4\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(Z)\frac{1}{12}}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}Z}.

Hence with (2.3), Lemma 2.7 finishes the proof of Theorem 2.3.

Proof of Lemma 2.7.

This part is rather technical, though quite elementary. For every integer m≥0m\geq 0, Fubini’s theorem gives

𝔼​Zm=𝔼​Ym+1−𝔼​Xm+1(m+1)​A.\mathbb{E}Z^{m}=\frac{\mathbb{E}Y^{m+1}-\mathbb{E}X^{m+1}}{(m+1)A}.

Indeed,

∫01xmΦ(x)dx=∫01xm𝔼𝟏{X≤x}dx=𝔼∫X1xmdx=1−𝔼​Xm+1m+1,\int_{0}^{1}x^{m}\Phi(x)\,dx=\int_{0}^{1}x^{m}\mathbb{E}\mathbf{1}_{\{X\leq x\}}\,dx=\mathbb{E}\int_{X}^{1}x^{m}\,dx=\frac{1-\mathbb{E}X^{m+1}}{m+1},

and since p=(Φ−Ψ)/Ap=(\Phi-\Psi)/A, the analogous identity for Ψ\Psi gives the claim after subtraction. What follows is mostly algebraic identities involving TT and SS.

Recall that X=T​UX=TU, and Y=1−S​VY=1-SV, and introduce

z=𝔼​T−𝔼​S2,e=𝔼⁡[T⁡(1−T)]+𝔼⁡[S⁡(1−S)],k=𝔼⁡[T⁡(1−T)]−𝔼⁡[S⁡(1−S)].z=\frac{\mathbb{E}T-\mathbb{E}S}{2},\quad e=\mathbb{E}[T(1-T)]+\mathbb{E}[S(1-S)],\quad k=\mathbb{E}[T(1-T)]-\mathbb{E}[S(1-S)].

𝔼​X2=𝔼⁡[T2]3,𝔼​Y2=1−𝔼​S+𝔼⁡[S2]3,\mathbb{E}X^{2}=\frac{\mathbb{E}[T^{2}]}{3},\qquad\mathbb{E}Y^{2}=1-\mathbb{E}S+\frac{\mathbb{E}[S^{2}]}{3},

we obtain

𝔼​Z=1−𝔼​S+13​(𝔼⁡[S2]−𝔼⁡[T2])2​A=12+z+k6​A.\mathbb{E}Z=\frac{1-\mathbb{E}S+\frac{1}{3}\bigl(\mathbb{E}[S^{2}]-\mathbb{E}[T^{2}]\bigr)}{2A}=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{z+k}{6A}.

Similarly, using the moment formula with m=2m=2,

𝔼​X3=𝔼⁡[T3]4,\mathbb{E}X^{3}=\frac{\mathbb{E}[T^{3}]}{4},

while

𝔼​Z2=1−32​𝔼​S+𝔼⁡[S2]−14​(𝔼⁡[S3]+𝔼⁡[T3])3​A.\mathbb{E}Z^{2}=\frac{1-\frac{3}{2}\mathbb{E}S+\mathbb{E}[S^{2}]-\frac{1}{4}\bigl(\mathbb{E}[S^{3}]+\mathbb{E}[T^{3}]\bigr)}{3A}.

Consequently,

𝔼​Z2=13+z+k6​A−𝔼⁡[T​(1−T)2]+𝔼⁡[S​(1−S)2]12​A.\mathbb{E}Z^{2}=\frac{1}{3}+\frac{z+k}{6A}-\frac{\mathbb{E}[T(1-T)^{2}]+\mathbb{E}[S(1-S)^{2}]}{12A}.

12​Var⁡Z=12​𝔼​Z2−12​(𝔼​Z)2=1−𝔼⁡[T​(1−T)2]+𝔼⁡[S​(1−S)2]A−(z+k)23​A2.12\operatorname{Var}Z=12\mathbb{E}Z^{2}-12(\mathbb{E}Z)^{2}=1-\frac{\mathbb{E}[T(1-T)^{2}]+\mathbb{E}[S(1-S)^{2}]}{A}-\frac{(z+k)^{2}}{3A^{2}}.

The analogous result for the second moment is immediate.

Corollary 2.8.

In the setting of Theorem 2.3, let QQ be a random variable with density qq, and let ZZ, as before, have density pp. Then Var⁡(Q)≥Var⁡(Z)\operatorname{Var}(Q)\geq\operatorname{Var}(Z).

Proof.

Indeed, we have 13​B≤𝒟⁡(q)≤23​Var⁡(Q)\frac{1}{3}B\leq\mathcal{D}(q)\leq\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(Q)}, therefore 12​Var⁡(Q)≥B212\operatorname{Var}(Q)\geq B^{2}. At the same time 12​Var⁡(Z)≤B212\operatorname{Var}(Z)\leq B^{2}, by Lemma 2.7. ∎

3 Proof of Theorem 1.2

Assume for now that KK is smooth and strictly convex. Fix a direction, normalize its projection to [0,1][0,1], and use the notation from the plan:

W=f−g,a=f′,b=g′.W=f-g,\qquad a=f^{\prime},\qquad b=g^{\prime}.

The functions aa and bb are respectively nonincreasing and nondecreasing, while

W′=a−b,W⁡(0)=W⁡(1)=0.W^{\prime}=a-b,\qquad W(0)=W(1)=0.

The normalized projected area density is

p⁡(x)=W⁡(x)𝒜,𝒜=∫01W⁡(x)​𝑑x.p(x)=\frac{W(x)}{\mathcal{A}},\qquad\mathcal{A}=\int_{0}^{1}W(x)\,dx. (3.1)

The unnormalized projected arclength boundary density is

r⁡(x)=1+a​(x)2+1+b​(x)2.r(x)=\sqrt{1+a(x)^{2}}+\sqrt{1+b(x)^{2}}.

Let

R=∫01r⁡(x)​𝑑x,R=\int_{0}^{1}r(x)\,dx,

so that the normalized projected boundary density is q⁡(x)=r⁡(x)R.q(x)=\frac{r(x)}{R}. Define

φ⁡(x)=1+a​(x)2+a⁡(x)+1+b​(x)2−b⁡(x)R\varphi(x)=\frac{\sqrt{1+a(x)^{2}}+a(x)+\sqrt{1+b(x)^{2}}-b(x)}{R}

and

ψ⁡(x)=1+a​(x)2−a⁡(x)+1+b​(x)2+b⁡(x)R.\psi(x)=\frac{\sqrt{1+a(x)^{2}}-a(x)+\sqrt{1+b(x)^{2}}+b(x)}{R}.

Clearly,

q=φ+ψ2.q=\frac{\varphi+\psi}{2}.

Since aa is nonincreasing and bb is nondecreasing, it follows that φ\varphi is nonincreasing and ψ\psi is nondecreasing. Both are nonnegative. Moreover,

∫01(a−b)​𝑑x=W⁡(1)−W⁡(0)=0,\int_{0}^{1}(a-b)\,dx=W(1)-W(0)=0,

and hence

∫01φ⁡(x)​𝑑x=1R​∫01(r⁡(x)+a⁡(x)−b⁡(x))​𝑑x=1,\int_{0}^{1}\varphi(x)\,dx=\frac{1}{R}\int_{0}^{1}\bigl(r(x)+a(x)-b(x)\bigr)\,dx=1,

and similarly

∫01ψ⁡(x)​𝑑x=1.\int_{0}^{1}\psi(x)\,dx=1.

Thus φ\varphi and ψ\psi are probability densities of the type appearing in Theorem 2.3.

Let Φ\Phi and Ψ\Psi be their distribution functions. Then

Φ⁡(x)−Ψ⁡(x)=2R​∫0x(a⁡(s)−b⁡(s))​𝑑s=2​W​(x)R.\Phi(x)-\Psi(x)=\frac{2}{R}\int_{0}^{x}(a(s)-b(s))\,ds=\frac{2W(x)}{R}.

Consequently,

∫01(Φ⁡(x)−Ψ⁡(x))​𝑑x=2​𝒜R,\int_{0}^{1}\bigl(\Phi(x)-\Psi(x)\bigr)\,dx=\frac{2\mathcal{A}}{R},

and therefore

Φ⁡(x)−Ψ⁡(x)∫01(Φ−Ψ)=W⁡(x)𝒜=p⁡(x).\frac{\Phi(x)-\Psi(x)}{\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}(\Phi-\Psi)}=\frac{W(x)}{\mathcal{A}}=p(x).

Since q=(φ+ψ)/2q=(\varphi+\psi)/2, Theorem 2.3 gives

𝒟⁡(q)≥𝒟⁡(p).\mathcal{D}(q)\geq\mathcal{D}(p).

This proves the directional inequality (1.1) for every smooth strictly convex planar body.

Let KnK_{n} be smooth strictly convex bodies converging to KK in the Hausdorff metric. Then the normalized area measures on KnK_{n} converge weakly to normalized area measure on KK, see e.g. [8]. Likewise, the normalized arclength measures on ∂Kn\partial K_{n} converge weakly to normalized arclength measure on ∂K\partial K; this follows from the weak continuity of curvature measures under Hausdorff convergence, see e.g. [7, 8]. Consequently, their pushforwards under x↦⟨x,u⟩x\mapsto\langle x,u\rangle converge weakly as well. Since all these measures are supported in a common compact interval, the Gini functionals converge, and passing to the limit proves the result for KK.

Remark 3.9.

One can avoid the approximation by keeping the vertical boundary faces as atoms at the endpoints of the projection interval. The limiting argument is used here only to keep the main exposition lighter.

Corollary 3.10.

For every planar convex body KK,

𝔼​|X1−X2|≤𝔼​|B1−B2|,\mathbb{E}|X_{1}-X_{2}|\leq\mathbb{E}|B_{1}-B_{2}|,

where X1,X2X_{1},X_{2} are uniform in KK and B1,B2B_{1},B_{2} are uniform on ∂K\partial K.

Proof.

Indeed, for normalized angular measure σ¯\bar{\sigma} on S1S^{1},

|z|=π2​∫S1|⟨z,u⟩|​𝑑σ¯​(u).|z|=\frac{\pi}{2}\int_{S^{1}}|\langle z,u\rangle|\,d\bar{\sigma}(u). (3.2)

See e.g. [8]. Integrating (3.2) against the two-point area and boundary distributions, and then using (1.1), gives the result. ∎

Corollary 3.11.

For every planar convex body KK,

𝔼​|X1−X2|2≤𝔼​|B1−B2|2,\mathbb{E}|X_{1}-X_{2}|^{2}\leq\mathbb{E}|B_{1}-B_{2}|^{2},

where X1,X2X_{1},X_{2} are uniform in KK and B1,B2B_{1},B_{2} are uniform on ∂K\partial K.

Proof.

For a smooth strictly convex body, the proof of Theorem 1.2 shows that, for every u∈S1u\in S^{1}, the projected area and boundary densities are obtained from the same pair of decreasing and increasing densities as in Theorem 2.3. Corollary 2.8 gives

Var⁡⟨X1,u⟩≤Var⁡⟨B1,u⟩.\operatorname{Var}\langle X_{1},u\rangle\leq\operatorname{Var}\langle B_{1},u\rangle.

Observe that

𝔼​⟨X1−X2,u⟩2=2​Var⁡⟨X1,u⟩,\mathbb{E}\langle X_{1}-X_{2},u\rangle^{2}=2\operatorname{Var}\langle X_{1},u\rangle,

and similarly

𝔼​⟨B1−B2,u⟩2=2​Var⁡⟨B1,u⟩.\mathbb{E}\langle B_{1}-B_{2},u\rangle^{2}=2\operatorname{Var}\langle B_{1},u\rangle.

Therefore

𝔼​⟨X1−X2,u⟩2≤𝔼​⟨B1−B2,u⟩2\mathbb{E}\langle X_{1}-X_{2},u\rangle^{2}\leq\mathbb{E}\langle B_{1}-B_{2},u\rangle^{2}

for every u∈S1u\in S^{1}.

For normalized angular measure σ¯\bar{\sigma} on S1S^{1},

|z|2=2​∫S1⟨z,u⟩2​𝑑σ¯​(u).|z|^{2}=2\int_{S^{1}}\langle z,u\rangle^{2}\,d\bar{\sigma}(u).

Integrating the preceding directional inequality over uu therefore gives

𝔼​|X1−X2|2≤𝔼​|B1−B2|2.\mathbb{E}|X_{1}-X_{2}|^{2}\leq\mathbb{E}|B_{1}-B_{2}|^{2}.

The general case follows by the same smooth approximation argument as in the proof of Theorem 1.2, since variance is continuous under weak convergence for measures supported in a common compact interval. ∎

4 A long-body observation

In this section, we construct a three-dimensional counterexample to the Zaporozhets-Tarasov conjecture, see Example 4.13. This example is then used to construct counterexamples in higher dimensions, see Proposition 4.16. The main observation, discussed in Remark 4.15, is that in dimension three the area and perimeter profiles of sections orthogonal to a fixed direction can be controlled almost independently. We exploit this freedom to make the projected Gini mean difference strictly larger for the volume measure than for the surface measure. A sufficiently large stretch in the projection direction then yields the required counterexample.

Lemma 4.12.

Suppose a random point has the form Z=(L​T,U)∈ℝ×ℝmZ=(LT,U)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{m}, where T∈[0,1]T\in[0,1] and the support of UU has diameter at most DD. If Z1,Z2Z_{1},Z_{2} are independent copies, then

L​𝔼​|T1−T2|≤𝔼​|Z1−Z2|≤L​𝔼​|T1−T2|+D.L\mathbb{E}|T_{1}-T_{2}|\leq\mathbb{E}|Z_{1}-Z_{2}|\leq L\mathbb{E}|T_{1}-T_{2}|+D.
Proof.

The lower bound follows by projection onto the first coordinate. For the upper bound, use

|(L⁡(T1−T2),U1−U2)|≤L​|T1−T2|+|U1−U2|.|(L(T_{1}-T_{2}),U_{1}-U_{2})|\leq L|T_{1}-T_{2}|+|U_{1}-U_{2}|.

∎

Thus, after division by LL, mean distances in a long body converge to mean absolute differences of the corresponding axial coordinates.

Remark 4.15.

Consider a long body with rectangular transverse sections

Qt=∏i=1d−1[−ai​(t),ai​(t)].Q_{t}=\prod_{i=1}^{d-1}[-a_{i}(t),a_{i}(t)].

Up to constant factors, the axial density of volume measure is

∏i=1d−1ai​(t),\prod_{i=1}^{d-1}a_{i}(t),

whereas the lateral surface density is

∑i=1d−1∏j≠iaj​(t).\sum_{i=1}^{d-1}\prod_{j\neq i}a_{j}(t).

In dimension three this is the difference between a product a1​a2a_{1}a_{2} and a sum a1+a2a_{1}+a_{2}. Choosing one width increasing and one decreasing can make the normalized surface density more concentrated along the long axis than the normalized volume density. In dimension two there is only one transverse width: the second expression is the empty product.

5 The lower bound for boundary mean distance

We now prove the lower estimate stated in the Introduction. The argument is again a comparison of one-dimensional distributions. Here the relevant laws are obtained by choosing either one random tangent direction or the median of three random tangent directions on a moving half-boundary.

Theorem 5.17.

For every planar convex body KK,

θ⁡(K)>per⁡K6.\theta(K)>\frac{\operatorname{per}K}{6}.

The constant 1/61/6 is sharp.

Assume first that ∂K\partial K is C2C^{2}, strictly convex, has positive curvature, and oriented counter-clockwise. Parameterize it by the tangent angle α∈ℝ/2​π​ℤ\alpha\in\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z}:

γ′​(α)=τ⁡(α)​(cos⁡α,sin⁡α),d​s=τ⁡(α)​d​α,\gamma^{\prime}(\alpha)=\tau(\alpha)(\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha),\qquad ds=\tau(\alpha)\,d\alpha, (5.1)

Proposition 5.19.

For every 0≤a≤π/20\leq a\leq\pi/2,

For a randomly chosen half-boundary, the median of three random points tends to move away from its ends. If both angular end-pieces [t,t+a][t,t+a] and [t+π−a,t+π][t+\pi-a,t+\pi] contain at most half of the arclength, this already gives the statement by pointwise comparison in tt. The difficulty is that tangent angle and arclength need not be distributed uniformly: a short angular end-piece may carry more than half of the arclength. Proof of this Proposition relies on the following Lemma.

Lemma 5.20.

Let μ\mu be a finite nonnegative Borel measure on the circle of circumference 2​h2h. Suppose 0<a≤b0<a\leq b and a+b=ha+b=h. For x<y≤x+2​hx<y\leq x+2h, write μ[x,y)\mu[x,y) for the μ\mu-mass of the positively oriented half-open arc from xx to yy. Put

Proof of Theorem 5.17.

As we outlined before Proposition 5.19,

∫02​πS(t)2𝔼sinItdt\displaystyle\int_{0}^{2\pi}S(t)^{2}\mathbb{E}\sin I_{t}\,dt =∫02​πS⁡(t)​(∫tt+πτ⁡(α)​sin⁡(α−t)​𝑑α)​𝑑t\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{2\pi}S(t)\left(\int_{t}^{t+\pi}\tau(\alpha)\sin(\alpha-t)\,d\alpha\right)dt (5.18)
=∫02​πS⁡(t)​w​(t)​dt,\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{2\pi}S(t)w(t)\,dt,

where w⁡(t)w(t) is the width of KK in direction utu_{t}. Indeed,

w⁡(t)=⟨γ⁡(t+π)−γ⁡(t),ut⟩=∫tt+π⟨γ′​(α),ut⟩​𝑑α=∫tt+πτ⁡(α)​sin⁡(α−t)​𝑑α.w(t)=\langle\gamma(t+\pi)-\gamma(t),u_{t}\rangle=\int_{t}^{t+\pi}\langle\gamma^{\prime}(\alpha),u_{t}\rangle d\alpha=\int_{t}^{t+\pi}\tau(\alpha)\sin(\alpha-t)d\alpha.

Since

S⁡(t)+S⁡(t+π)=P,w⁡(t+π)=w⁡(t),S(t)+S(t+\pi)=P,\qquad w(t+\pi)=w(t),

Cauchy’s perimeter formula gives

∫02​πS⁡(t)​w​(t)​𝑑t=P​∫0πw⁡(t)​𝑑t=P2.\int_{0}^{2\pi}S(t)w(t)\,dt=P\int_{0}^{\pi}w(t)\,dt=P^{2}. (5.19)

Combining Propositions 5.18 and  5.19 with (5.19), we obtain

θ⁡(K)≥P6.\theta(K)\geq\frac{P}{6}.

By smooth approximation, the same chain of inequalities holds for every planar convex body, with τ⁡(α)​d​α\tau(\alpha)d\alpha replaced by its tangent-angle measure. Thus θ⁡(K)≥P/6\theta(K)\geq P/6 in general. It remains to exclude equality for a nondegenerate convex body. Suppose therefore that

θ⁡(K)=P6.\theta(K)=\frac{P}{6}.

Then both inequalities supplied by Propositions 5.2 and 5.3 must be equalities.

Let μ\mu be the tangent-angle measure of ∂K\partial K. We first observe that equality in Proposition 5.3 implies that no open semicircle contains three points of supp⁡μ\operatorname{supp}\mu. Indeed, suppose that, after lifting the angles to ℝ\mathbb{R},

0=x<z<y=d<π,x,z,y∈supp⁡μ.0=x<z<y=d<\pi,\qquad x,z,y\in\operatorname{supp}\mu.

Choose a>0a>0 so small that

a<z,a<π−d,a<z,\qquad a<\pi-d,

and put b=π−ab=\pi-a. Then Ta(d)=(−a,0],δ=b−dT_{a}(d)=(-a,0],\,\delta=b-d. The cut points of aa- and bb-splittings are q=t+aq=t+a and q′=t′+b=t+dq^{\prime}=t^{\prime}+b=t+d, respectively. Now, we want zz to lie strictly between them. For that purpose any tt in the non-empty interval (max⁡{−a,z−d},0)(\max\left\{-a,z-d\right\},0) works. For every such tt the inequality

μ[q,t+h)μ[t,t+h)≥μ[q′,t+h)μ[t,t+h)\frac{\mu[q,t+h)}{\mu[t,t+h)}\geq\frac{\mu[q^{\prime},t+h)}{\mu[t,t+h)}

is in fact strict, since z∈[q,q′)z\in[q,q^{\prime}). The same remains true for xx and yy in sufficiently small neighborhoods of the chosen points. Consequently,

Fa,b​(μ)<Fb,a​(μ).F_{a,b}(\mu)<F_{b,a}(\mu).

Moreover, this remains strict for all aa in a sufficiently small open interval. That makes inequality 5.10 strict. Now, we have shown that

|supp⁡μ|≤4.|\operatorname{supp}\mu|\leq 4.

Indeed, if five points occurred in cyclic order and g1,…,g5g_{1},\ldots,g_{5} were the intervening angular gaps, then the absence of three points in an open semicircle would imply

gi+gi+1≥π(i(mod5)).g_{i}+g_{i+1}\geq\pi\qquad(i\!\!\!\pmod{5}).

Summing gives 4​π≥5​π4\pi\geq 5\pi, since ∑igi=2​π\sum_{i}g_{i}=2\pi, which is impossible.

Hence KK is a polygon with at most four sides. We now show that Proposition 5.2 is strict for every nondegenerate polygon. Choose an open interval JJ of angles tt so that for every t∈Jt\in J

ut=(−sin⁡t,cos⁡t)u_{t}=(-\sin t,\cos t)

is not normal to any edge of KK. For t∈Jt\in J the linear functional x↦⟨x,ut⟩x\mapsto\langle x,u_{t}\rangle attains its minimum and maximum at unique vertices vv and ww, respectively. Those vertices split ∂K\partial K in two complementary polygonal chains. Denote their lengths by S1,S2S_{1},S_{2}, and let ν1,t,ν2,t\nu_{1,t},\nu_{2,t} be their normalized arclength measures projected onto utu_{t}.

The equality in the concavity step of Proposition 5.2 is equivalent to

ν1,t=ν2,t.\nu_{1,t}=\nu_{2,t}.

Let e1,e2e_{1},e_{2} be the unit vectors along the edges of the two chains incident to vv and directed away from vv. For t∈Jt\in J,

⟨ei,ut⟩>0.\langle e_{i},u_{t}\rangle>0.

Near the projection of vv, the densities of ν1,t\nu_{1,t} and ν2,t\nu_{2,t} are respectively

1S1​⟨e1,ut⟩,1S2​⟨e2,ut⟩.\frac{1}{S_{1}\langle e_{1},u_{t}\rangle},\qquad\frac{1}{S_{2}\langle e_{2},u_{t}\rangle}.

Therefore equality of the two projected laws would imply

⟨S1​e1−S2​e2,ut⟩=0.\bigl\langle S_{1}e_{1}-S_{2}e_{2},u_{t}\bigr\rangle=0.

As S1​e1−S2​e2≠0S_{1}e_{1}-S_{2}e_{2}\neq 0, this can hold only for isolated values of tt, whereas JJ is an interval. Hence the Gini concavity inequality is strict on a set of positive measure, and so Proposition 5.2 is strict for every nondegenerate polygon.

Therefore,

θ⁡(K)>per⁡K6.\theta(K)>\frac{\operatorname{per}K}{6}.

Sharpness follows from the rectangles Kε=[0,1]×[0,ε]K_{\varepsilon}=[0,1]\times[0,\varepsilon]. As ε↓0\varepsilon\downarrow 0, normalized boundary arclength concentrates on the two horizontal sides, and hence θ⁡(Kε)→𝔼​|U−V|=1/3\theta(K_{\varepsilon})\to\mathbb{E}|U-V|=1/3, where U,V∼Unif⁡[0,1]U,V\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1], while per⁡Kε→2\operatorname{per}K_{\varepsilon}\to 2. ∎

6 Note added

After the first version of our work was posted on arXiv, two related independent works became publicly available. Kukushkin [9] gave a proof of Theorem 2.3 and the planar Zaporozhets–Tarasov conjecture using a quite different approach. Lotnikov [10], whose work is based on his bachelor’s thesis defended in June 2026, constructed centrally symmetric counterexamples in every dimension d≥3d\geq 3, for every moment of the distance. These results overlap, respectively, with our Theorem 1.2 and the higher-dimensional counterexamples.

8 Declaration of AI use

The author used ChatGPT with the GPT-5.6 Sol model during the preparation of this work. The first proof of the planar case of Zaporozhets-Tarasov conjecture, namely Theorem 1.2, was obtained by the author without the use of AI tools; it was based on KKT conditions and an exhaustive case analysis and was substantially more technical. The argument was subsequently simplified through discussions with ChatGPT. The author also used ChatGPT to search for the explicit construction in Example 4.2 from the author’s underlying idea described in Remark 4.15 (that includes generation of relevant code). The author reviewed and verified all AI-assisted output and takes full responsibility for the content of the article.

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
